questions.stem: A 68-year-old man comes to the emergency department with 2 days of palpitations. Pulse is 150/min and regular. Blood pressure is 128/80 mm Hg. ECG shows a regular narrow-QRS tachycardia at 150/min. A dose of IV adenosine slows the ventricular rate for a few seconds. During this pause, regular sawtooth waves at about 300/min are clearly seen in leads II, III and aVF. Then the ventricular rate returns to 150/min. A cardiologist plans a catheter ablation to cure this rhythm. Ablation of which structure is most likely to cure it?
choices: Slow pathway of the AV node
Muscle sleeves around the pulmonary vein ostia
Accessory pathway at the mitral annulus
questions.explanation: Adenosine briefly blocks the AV node and **unmasks the flutter waves**: this is **typical atrial flutter** with **2:1 conduction**. The circuit is a **macroreentry** around the tricuspid annulus in the right atrium, and ablating the **cavotricuspid isthmus** breaks it. Pulmonary vein isolation is tempting, but those veins hold the triggers of **atrial fibrillation**, not this right atrial circuit. Ablation of the His bundle only controls the ventricular rate (it needs a pacemaker) and leaves the atria in flutter.
questions.explanation_pt: A adenosina bloqueia o nó AV por alguns segundos e **revela as ondas F**: trata-se de **flutter atrial típico** com **condução 2:1**. O circuito é uma **macrorreentrada** ao redor do anel tricúspide no átrio direito, e a ablação do **istmo cavotricuspídeo** o interrompe. O isolamento das veias pulmonares é tentador, mas essas veias contêm os gatilhos da **FA**, e não deste circuito do átrio direito. A ablação do feixe de His apenas controla a frequência ventricular (exige marca-passo) e deixa os átrios em flutter.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with COPD comes to the emergency department with sudden palpitations that started 40 minutes ago. Pulse is 186/min and regular. Blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg. ECG shows a regular narrow-QRS tachycardia with no visible P waves. Vagal maneuvers do not work. She receives the usual doses of IV adenosine by rapid push, but the rhythm does not change. Her home medicines include an inhaled bronchodilator and oral theophylline. Which mechanism best explains the lack of response to adenosine?
choices: Theophylline blocks adenosine receptors in the AV node
Theophylline induces liver enzymes that clear adenosine
Theophylline blocks the cellular uptake of adenosine
Theophylline increases acetylcholine release at the AV node
questions.explanation: **Theophylline** (like caffeine) is a **methylxanthine** that **blocks adenosine receptors**, so adenosine cannot activate the A1 receptors that slow AV nodal conduction and break the **reentry circuit**. Adenosine is not cleared by the liver: red cells and endothelium take it up and break it down within seconds, so enzyme induction plays no role. Blocking adenosine uptake is the action of **dipyridamole**, and it makes the effect of adenosine stronger, not weaker.
questions.explanation_pt: A **teofilina** (assim como a cafeína) é uma **metilxantina** que **bloqueia os receptores de adenosina**, então a adenosina não consegue ativar os receptores A1 que retardam a condução no nó AV e interrompem o **circuito de reentrada**. A adenosina não é depurada pelo fígado: hemácias e endotélio a captam e a degradam em segundos, então a indução enzimática não tem papel. Bloquear a captação de adenosina é a ação do **dipiridamol**, que torna o efeito da adenosina mais forte, e não mais fraco.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old man from Vietnam is brought to the emergency department after he fainted at home. He has had a fever for 2 days from a viral illness. His older brother died suddenly in his sleep at age 35. Vital signs: temperature 39.0 °C, pulse 96/min, blood pressure 122/78 mm Hg, respiratory rate 16/min. ECG shows an rSR' pattern in V1 and V2 with coved ST elevation in V1-V3 that slopes down into inverted T waves. The QT interval is normal. Troponin is normal. A loss-of-function mutation in which protein most likely causes this condition?
choices: Ryanodine receptor of the sarcoplasmic reticulum
questions.explanation: A young man of Asian origin with syncope, a family history of **sudden death during sleep** and a **pseudo-right bundle branch block** with **ST elevation in V1-V3** has **Brugada syndrome**. It is most often linked to **loss of function of the cardiac Na+ channel**, and **fever** can unmask the ECG pattern and trigger VF. Loss of function of the IKs or IKr K+ channels causes congenital **long QT**, but his QT is normal. The definitive protection against sudden death is an **ICD**.
questions.explanation_pt: Um homem jovem de origem asiática com síncope, história familiar de **morte súbita durante o sono** e **padrão de pseudobloqueio de ramo direito** com **supradesnivelamento do ST em V1-V3** tem **síndrome de Brugada**. Ela está associada principalmente à **perda de função do canal de Na+ cardíaco**, e a **febre** pode revelar o padrão no ECG e desencadear FV. A perda de função dos canais de K+ IKs ou IKr causa **QT longo** congênito, mas o QT dele é normal. A proteção definitiva contra a morte súbita é o **CDI**.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl is evaluated after two fainting episodes: one while swimming and one while running in a race. She has been deaf since birth and uses a cochlear implant. Her parents are first cousins. Both parents have normal hearing and have never fainted. Her ECG shows sinus rhythm with a markedly prolonged QT interval. Serum potassium, magnesium and calcium are normal, and she takes no medicines. Which inheritance pattern is most likely?
questions.explanation: **Congenital sensorineural deafness** plus a **long QT** with exercise-triggered syncope is **Jervell and Lange-Nielsen syndrome**, which is **autosomal recessive**; parents who are relatives and unaffected fit this pattern. The defective K+ channel (IKs) is also needed for normal potassium handling in the inner ear, which explains the deafness. **Romano-Ward** syndrome is the tempting choice, but it is autosomal dominant and hearing is normal.
questions.explanation_pt: **Surdez neurossensorial congênita** com **QT longo** e síncope desencadeada por exercício é a **síndrome de Jervell e Lange-Nielsen**, de herança **autossômica recessiva**; pais consanguíneos e não afetados se encaixam nesse padrão. O canal de K+ defeituoso (IKs) também é necessário para o manejo normal do potássio na orelha interna, o que explica a surdez. A síndrome de **Romano-Ward** é a opção tentadora, mas é autossômica dominante e a audição é normal.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man comes to the emergency department with 2 hours of crushing chest pain. Pulse is 52/min and irregular. Blood pressure is 104/66 mm Hg. ECG shows ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF. A rhythm strip shows the following PR intervals in a repeating cycle: 0.16 s, then 0.24 s, then 0.28 s, then a P wave with no QRS after it. The cycle then starts again at 0.16 s. Occlusion of which artery most likely explains both the infarct and the conduction problem?
questions.explanation: The PR lengthens beat by beat until a QRS drops: **Mobitz I (Wenckebach)**, a block at the level of the **AV node**. In most people (right-dominant circulation) the **AV nodal artery** arises from the **right coronary artery**, which also supplies the inferior wall, so an **inferior MI** with Wenckebach points to the RCA. The left circumflex can cause an inferior MI in a left-dominant heart, but this is much less common. LAD occlusion causes an anterior MI and, when it damages the conduction system, a block below the AV node (Mobitz II or complete block).
questions.explanation_pt: O PR aumenta batimento a batimento até um QRS falhar: **Mobitz I (Wenckebach)**, um bloqueio no nível do **nó AV**. Na maioria das pessoas (dominância direita), a **artéria do nó AV** nasce da **artéria coronária direita**, que também irriga a parede inferior; por isso, um **IAM inferior** com Wenckebach aponta para a coronária direita. A circunflexa pode causar IAM inferior num coração com dominância esquerda, mas isso é bem menos comum. A oclusão da descendente anterior causa IAM anterior e, quando lesa o sistema de condução, um bloqueio abaixo do nó AV (Mobitz II ou BAV total).

questions.stem: An 81-year-old woman has had several episodes of light-headedness and one fall over the past 2 months. She takes no medicines, and her TSH is normal. A 24-hour Holter monitor shows: sinus rhythm at 42-48/min for most of the day, rising only to 58/min while she walks; several runs of atrial fibrillation at 130-150/min; and, when each run of atrial fibrillation stops, a pause of about 4.5 seconds with no P waves and no QRS complexes before the next sinus beat. Her dizziness matches these pauses. Every P wave is followed by a QRS complex with a constant PR interval of 0.18 s. Which diagnosis is most likely?
choices: Second-degree AV block, Mobitz type II
Atrial fibrillation with slow ventricular response
questions.explanation: Slow sinus rhythm that barely rises with effort, runs of atrial fibrillation, and long **sinus pauses** when the tachycardia stops form the **tachy-brady syndrome** of **sick sinus syndrome**. It is usually due to age-related **fibrosis of the sinus node**, and symptomatic patients need a **pacemaker**. Mobitz II and complete AV block are tempting, but in those disorders P waves still appear and fail to conduct; here there are no P waves during the pauses, and every P wave is conducted.
questions.explanation_pt: Ritmo sinusal lento que quase não aumenta com o esforço, episódios de FA e **pausas sinusais** longas quando a taquicardia termina formam a **síndrome bradicardia-taquicardia** da **doença do nó sinusal**. Ela geralmente decorre de **fibrose do nó sinusal** relacionada à idade, e os pacientes sintomáticos precisam de **marca-passo**. O Mobitz II e o BAV total são tentadores, mas neles as ondas P continuam aparecendo e não são conduzidas; aqui não há ondas P durante as pausas, e toda onda P é conduzida.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman with hypertension and type 2 diabetes is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after sudden weakness of her left arm and slurred speech. Vital signs: pulse 112/min and irregularly irregular, blood pressure 150/88 mm Hg, temperature 36.8 °C. No murmur is heard. ECG shows atrial fibrillation and no Q waves. Transthoracic echocardiography shows normal left ventricular wall motion, an ejection fraction of 60%, an enlarged left atrium, no valve vegetations, and no shunt on a bubble study. Carotid ultrasound shows less than 30% stenosis on both sides. Where did the embolus most likely form?
questions.explanation: In **atrial fibrillation** the atria quiver and do not contract in an organized way, so blood **stagnates**, and a thrombus forms mostly in the **left atrial appendage**; it can embolize to the brain (**cardioembolic stroke**). A left ventricular apical thrombus is tempting, but it usually follows a large anterior MI with poor wall motion, and her wall motion is normal. A leg-vein clot reaches the brain only through a shunt (paradoxical embolism), which the bubble study excluded. **Anticoagulation** is used to lower this risk.
questions.explanation_pt: Na **FA** os átrios fibrilam e não se contraem de forma organizada, então o sangue fica **estagnado** e forma-se um trombo principalmente no **apêndice atrial esquerdo**; ele pode embolizar para o cérebro (**AVC cardioembólico**). Um trombo no ápice do ventrículo esquerdo é tentador, mas costuma ocorrer após um grande IAM anterior com déficit de contratilidade segmentar, e a contratilidade segmentar dela é normal. Um trombo de veia da perna só chega ao cérebro por um shunt (embolia paradoxal), que o teste de microbolhas excluiu. A **anticoagulação** é usada para reduzir esse risco.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with sudden palpitations. An ECG from a routine visit last year showed a PR interval of 0.10 s and a slurred upstroke of the QRS complex. Today her pulse is 210/min and regular, and her blood pressure is 112/70 mm Hg. ECG shows a regular tachycardia with narrow QRS complexes and no slurred upstroke. Inverted P waves are seen in the ST segment shortly after each QRS complex in leads II, III and aVF. Which route does the electrical impulse most likely follow during this tachycardia?
choices: Down the AV node and back up the accessory pathway
Down the accessory pathway and back up the AV node
Around a circuit inside the AV node only
Around the tricuspid annulus in the right atrium
Around a scar in the ventricular muscle
questions.explanation: She has **Wolff-Parkinson-White** (short PR and delta wave at baseline). The most common tachycardia in WPW is **orthodromic AV reentrant tachycardia**: the impulse goes **down the AV node** and the His-Purkinje system, so the QRS is **narrow** with no delta wave, and then **back up the accessory pathway** to the atria, giving retrograde P waves just after the QRS. The reverse route (antidromic) is tempting, but it activates the ventricles through the accessory pathway and gives a **wide**, fully pre-excited QRS. In AV nodal reentry the retrograde P wave is usually hidden inside the QRS.
questions.explanation_pt: Ela tem **Wolff-Parkinson-White** (PR curto e onda delta no ECG basal). A taquicardia mais comum na síndrome de WPW é a **taquicardia por reentrada AV ortodrômica**: o impulso **desce pelo nó AV** e pelo sistema His-Purkinje, então o QRS é **estreito** e sem onda delta, e depois **sobe pela via acessória** até os átrios, gerando ondas P retrógradas logo após o QRS. A via inversa (antidrômica) é tentadora, mas ativa os ventrículos pela via acessória e gera um QRS **largo**, totalmente pré-excitado. Na reentrada nodal, a onda P retrógrada geralmente fica escondida dentro do QRS.
